source_title: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles; Search Warrant; Exceptions
citation: IC 35-33-5-9 (as added by P.L.170-2014, SEC.19; amended by P.L.57-2016, SEC.2; P.L.136-2019, SEC.1)
uas_topic: Law-enforcement UAV use restriction; private-property search/surveillance warrant requirement
regulated_activity: Using an unmanned aerial vehicle on or over private property, or to conduct a search, perform surveillance, or obtain a photograph or video of private property or of individuals, items, or structures on private property
requirement_type: Search-warrant requirement, with an exception where a warrant would not be required for the same search if conducted without a UAV
summary: IC 35-33-5-9 requires a law enforcement officer to obtain a search warrant to use an unmanned aerial vehicle (1) on or over private property, or (2) to search, surveil, photograph, or video private property or persons/items/structures on private property, without the affected owner's consent. A warrant is not required if one would not be required for the same search conducted without a UAV. The statute does not itself regulate private/commercial UAS operators.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Design acquisition and data-handling workflows to minimize unnecessary capture of people and private activity. Confirm the source-supported consent or project-purpose basis before flight and carry that limitation through processing, access control, retention, and delivery.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This authority governs a public entity rather than private operators directly. Review the solicitation and contract for incorporation or flow-down before treating it as binding on the consultant, and document the basis for that conclusion.

source_title: Voyeurism; Public Voyeurism; Aerial Voyeurism (Remote Aerial Voyeurism provisions)
citation: IC 35-45-4-5(g)-(h) (remote aerial voyeurism subsections added by P.L.107-2017)
revision_date: Unknown (current text shown current as of Jan. 1, 2026 per FindLaw codification mirror)
regulated_activity: Operating a UAV with intent to peep, causing it to enter the airspace above or surrounding another person's occupied dwelling to capture images, photographs, video, or audio of that person while in the dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area
requirement_type: Prohibition (Class A misdemeanor; Level 6 felony if a prior unrelated conviction, or if the images/recordings are published, posted online, or transmitted to another person)
summary: IC 35-45-4-5(g) makes it remote aerial voyeurism for a person, with intent to peep, to operate a UAV so that it enters the airspace above or surrounding another person's occupied dwelling to capture images, photographs, video, or audio of that person while inside the dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area, without consent. Subsection (h) elevates the offense to a Level 6 felony for a repeat offense or if the material is published, posted online, or transmitted to another person. This is a subsection within Indiana's broader voyeurism statute (Sec. 5), distinct from the separate remote aerial harassment offense at IC 35-45-10-6 (IN-003).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not operate a UAV with intent to peep or capture images of a person inside an occupied dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area, without consent -- this is a felony-eligible offense distinct from the broader voyeurism statute. Routine AEC survey, inspection, and mapping photography is not the conduct this subsection targets, but frame flight paths and camera angles to avoid incidental capture into private dwelling interiors, and never publish, post, or transmit any such incidental capture given subsection (h)'s felony-elevation trigger for publication.

source_title: Trafficking With an Inmate; Carrying Contraband Into a Correctional Facility / Trafficking With an Inmate Outside a Facility (UAV-delivered contraband)
citation: IC 35-44.1-3-5 and IC 35-44.1-3-6 (both amended by P.L.22-2024, part of Senate Enrolled Act 182, signed 2024-03-11)
regulated_activity: Delivering, carrying, or receiving contraband or another article to or from an inmate of a penal/juvenile facility, or delivering/placing contraband for an inmate being transported outside a facility, including by means of an unmanned aerial vehicle, without the facility head's prior authorization
requirement_type: Prohibition (Class A misdemeanor; Level 5 felony if the article is a controlled substance, chemical intoxicant, deadly weapon, or wireless device; Level 6 or Level 5 felony under Sec. 6 depending on contraband type)
permit_or_approval_required: N/A (facility head's prior authorization is the only avoidance mechanism)
summary: IC 35-44.1-3-5 makes it trafficking with an inmate, a Class A misdemeanor (Level 5 felony for certain contraband), to deliver, carry, or receive an article to or from an inmate or juvenile-facility resident without the facility head's prior authorization, expressly including delivery, carrying, or receipt 'through the use of an unmanned aerial vehicle.' IC 35-44.1-3-6 creates a parallel offense, trafficking with an inmate outside a facility, for delivering or placing contraband where an inmate being transported outside a facility could obtain it, likewise expressly including delivery or placement by UAV. Both sections were amended in 2024 (P.L.22-2024) as part of Senate Enrolled Act 182, enacted after the Indiana Department of Correction reported more than 30 drone sightings and over a dozen confirmed drone-delivered contraband drops at state correctional facilities in 2023.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Secure the facility head's prior written authorization before any UAV flight at or near a correctional or juvenile facility, regardless of the flight's purpose -- the statute's prior-authorization requirement is the only avoidance mechanism and applies to any person, not just inmates or visitors. Confirm the facility's specific point of contact, required lead time, and any site-specific conditions well before mobilization.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact the protected facility's owner, operator, administrator, commander, or other official identified by the authority before mobilization and ask whether the proposed AEC mission qualifies for written approval or an employment/contractor exception. Provide the site, purpose, dates, flight area, crew and aircraft details the facility requests, and retain the signed authorization and security conditions; do not assume ordinary site access or a client work order is sufficient.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Make the required approval and compliance with its conditions a documented mobilization gate. Allocate responsibility for applications and schedule impacts in the contract, and obtain counsel if the project's facts do not fit the stated authorization pathway.
verification_status: Full current text of both sections verified directly against Justia's Indiana Code mirror; the 2024 UAV-specific amendment (P.L.22-2024) is confirmed in each section's own history note and corroborated by contemporaneous news coverage of Senate Enrolled Act 182's March 11, 2024 signing.
notes: Codification of 2024's Senate Enrolled Act 182. AEC firms conducting authorized inspection, mapping, or documentation flights at or near a correctional facility should secure the facility head's advance authorization referenced in these sections before flying, to avoid inadvertent exposure to this offense.

issuing_authority: Indiana General Assembly / Indiana DNR (Division of Fish & Wildlife, enforcement)
source_title: Use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles to Aid Hunting
uas_topic: UAV-aided-hunting restriction (wildlife/hunting), with agricultural-monitoring and post-harvest-recovery exceptions
regulated_party: Hunters and the general public (exceptions for DNR and its designees, government agents, educational/research institutions, veterinary care, and agricultural/nuisance-animal monitoring)
regulated_activity: Using a UAV to search for, scout, locate, or detect a wild animal to which a hunting season applies, as an aid to taking that animal, during the period beginning 14 days before the season and running through its last legal hunting hour
requirement_type: Prohibition during the defined season window; UAV-aided recovery of an already-legally-taken animal (including with infrared) is expressly permitted, but does not authorize entering another's property without permission
summary: IC 14-22-6-16(c) prohibits knowingly using a UAV to search for, scout, locate, or detect a wild animal covered by a hunting season, as an aid to taking it, during a window beginning 14 days before that season and ending at the close of legal hunting hours on the season's last day. Subsection (d) permits using a UAV with infrared capability to locate and recover an already-legally-taken animal, but does not authorize entering another person's property without the landowner's permission. Subsection (a) exempts the department and its designees, government-agency employees/agents performing official duties, educational/research institution personnel for bona fide purposes, UAV use to assist or provide veterinary care to a specific wild animal, and UAV use to monitor agricultural production or nuisance wild animals.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental and mapping flights to avoid conduct that could be characterized as locating, pursuing, disturbing, or harassing wildlife. Coordinate mission timing and stand-off distances with the land manager when project work overlaps sensitive habitat or hunting activity.

jurisdiction_name: Indiana (DNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property statewide, including state parks, state forests, state recreation areas, nature preserves, fish and wildlife areas, and reservoir properties)
issuing_authority: Indiana Natural Resources Commission / Indiana Department of Natural Resources
source_title: Vehicles, Trails, Boats, and Aircraft -- Airborne-Device Prohibition on DNR Property
citation: 312 IAC 8-2-8(i) (Natural Resources Commission rule; most recently amended/readopted per filing 1/25/2024, eff. 20240221-IR-312230538FRA)
effective_date: Unknown original adoption date (rule filed Oct. 28, 1998, eff. Jan. 1, 1999); most recently amended effective per Feb. 2024 filing
uas_topic: State park/public land UAV landing and launch prohibition
regulated_party: Any person, including AEC/commercial UAS operators
regulated_activity: Landing, taxiing, taking off, parking, or mooring an unmanned motor-driven airborne device (or an airborne human transportation device) on DNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property
requirement_type: Prohibition except at a site designated by the Department for that purpose; DNR's own published guidance separately describes a discretionary launch/film licensing practice administered by DNR or a specific DNR division
permit_or_approval_required: Yes -- per DNR's own published guidance, a discretionary license from DNR or the relevant DNR division, plus an FAA license and proof of insurance, may be required outside a designated site; contact the property manager
summary: 312 IAC 8-2-8(i) prohibits a person from landing, taxiing, taking off, parking, or mooring an unmanned motor-driven airborne device, or an airborne human transportation device, on DNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property, except at a site the Department has designated for that purpose. The rule's own text contains no enumerated exceptions. This retrofit pass located and directly fetched DNR's own official implementing guidance -- State Form 56490's 'Commercial Film and Photography Application and Agreement Instructions' (in.gov/dnr) -- which resolves the citation discrepancy flagged in the original pass. DNR's own guidance confirms drones are 'generally prohibited on DNR properties to protect the privacy and safety of our guests and to protect the facilities and natural and cultural resources we conserve,' but describes four specific exception categories, each still requiring advance permit-application review, providing a copy of the drone operator's FAA license, and (for three of the four) proof of insurance: (1) professional journalists working on pieces informing the public about natural/cultural resources or agency activities (a commercial filming application is not typically required); (2) university researchers with an appropriate DNR research permit, where the drone use is warranted by the project design; (3) documentary filmmakers producing a non-for-profit documentary about DNR-managed resources, staff, or facilities, in association with a news agency or nonprofit (a commercial filming application is required); and (4) state, regional, or county tourism agencies or their partners producing promotional film, video, or still photography (a commercial filming application is required). This is a more precise and complete picture than either the rule's own bare text or the secondary drone-law aggregator sites' abbreviated three-category description (which omitted the documentary-filmmaker category and did not distinguish which categories require a full commercial filming application).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not assume any of the four DNR exception categories applies to standard AEC survey, mapping, or inspection work -- none of them cover commercial engineering, construction, or infrastructure-inspection UAS use. Treat any DNR-property launch or landing for AEC purposes as requiring a site-specific request to the property manager well in advance (DNR recommends 90 days for filming/photography permits), since AEC work does not fit any of the four enumerated categories and would need to be evaluated case-by-case.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact the relevant DNR division directly based on property type: the Outreach Coordinator (317-233-3864) for state parks, reservoirs, state recreation areas, and off-road riding areas; the Assistant State Forester (317-232-4101) for state forests; or the Assistant Director for Public Lands (317-232-8059) for fish & wildlife areas and dedicated nature preserves. Submit the DNR Commercial Film and Photography Agreement, provide the drone operator's FAA license and proof of insurance where the request falls within one of the four recognized exception categories, and budget at least 90 days for review given DNR's own stated processing expectations.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: The rule's bare text (312 IAC 8-2-8(i)) is an unqualified prohibition with no textual exceptions; DNR's discretionary exception practice is documented in agency guidance (State Form 56490 instructions), not the rule itself, so it should be treated as agency policy subject to change rather than a codified right. Confirm current DNR practice directly before advising a client that any exception category applies to a specific AEC engagement.
verification_status: Full current rule text (subsection (i)) verified directly against Cornell LII's mirror of 312 IAC 8-2-8 in the original pass. In this retrofit pass, DNR's own official implementing guidance (State Form 56490 Instructions, fetched directly from in.gov/dnr) was located and read in full, resolving the prior citation/discrepancy flag: it confirms four specific drone exception categories (professional journalists, university researchers, documentary filmmakers, and tourism agencies), each requiring advance permit review, an FAA license, and (for three of four) proof of insurance -- a more complete and precise picture than the three-category description found on secondary drone-law aggregator sites in the original pass.
notes: RESOLVED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS: the prior citation/discrepancy flag is superseded by direct verification of DNR's own official guidance document. Secondary drone-law aggregator sites' three-category description (journalists, researchers, tourism agencies) was substantially accurate but incomplete -- it omitted the documentary-filmmaker category and did not distinguish which categories require a full commercial filming application versus advance coordination only.

issuing_authority: Indiana General Assembly / Indiana State Police
citation: IC 10-22 (new article added by Senate Bill 227, 2026 Reg. Sess.; ceremonially signed by Governor Braun April 23, 2026; eff. 2026-07-01)
status: Current / in force (effective date passed; the federal trigger has since been satisfied -- see notes)
uas_topic: Counter-UAS (detection/mitigation) statewide coordination; critical-infrastructure/correctional-facility/airport 'high-risk site' designation; procurement restricted to the federal C-UAS Technology List
regulated_party: Indiana State Police (statewide coordinating agency); designated local law-enforcement 'participating agencies'
regulated_activity: State police authority to apply for federal counter-UAS authorization, coordinate detection/tracking/identification/mitigation activity by trained personnel, designate 'high-risk sites' (large public events, federally-rated special events, critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports) and a pilot-project location (Indianapolis), and restrict counter-UAS procurement to systems on the federal C-UAS Technology List
requirement_type: Authorizing/coordinating framework -- by its own terms (Article 22, Ch. 1), the article's substantive counter-UAS authority applies only once a triggering federal law is enacted and the Governor publishes notice in the Indiana Register
permit_or_approval_required: N/A (governs state agency authority, not private-operator permitting)
summary: New IC Article 10-22, added by Senate Bill 227 (2026 Reg. Sess.), designates the Indiana State Police as the statewide coordinating agency for counter-UAS activities authorized under federal law. It authorizes the state police to seek federal authorization to acquire, deploy, and operate counter-UAS systems; to designate local law-enforcement 'participating agencies' meeting federal training/readiness requirements; to designate Indianapolis as a pilot-project location given its concentration of high-risk sites; and to designate 'high-risk sites' including critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports, and large public/special-event-rated events. Counter-UAS systems must appear on the federal C-UAS Technology List. By its own terms (Chapter 1), the article applies only once a federal law authorizing state/local detection, tracking, identification, or mitigation of UAS is enacted and the Governor has published notice of that authorization in the Indiana Register; mitigation activity is barred absent express federal authorization.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This article governs Indiana State Police and designated local law-enforcement counter-UAS authority, not private AEC operators -- it does not restrict where or how an AEC firm may fly. The practical relevance is airspace/operational awareness: at any of the article's designated 'high-risk sites' (critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports, large public/special-rated events) or in the Indianapolis pilot-project area, confirm with the site owner or event organizer whether counter-UAS detection or mitigation activity may be active before mobilizing, since a legitimate AEC flight could be misidentified as a threat.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: This equipment restriction governs agency counter-UAS systems, not ordinary AEC aircraft or payloads. Do not treat it as a fleet-eligibility rule unless the contract requires the firm to furnish detection or mitigation technology.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Make the required approval and compliance with its conditions a documented mobilization gate. Allocate responsibility for applications and schedule impacts in the contract, and obtain counsel if the project's facts do not fit the stated authorization pathway.
verification_status: Full bill text (as reported favorably out of committee, Jan. 21, 2026, reflecting the enacted new-article structure) verified directly against an official Indiana General Assembly legislative document; the bill's passage and the Governor's April 23, 2026 ceremonial signing are corroborated by an Indiana House Republicans caucus press release. The final codified IC 10-22 text was not independently re-verified against a post-enactment primary codification mirror as of the date accessed.
notes: UPDATED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS: the article's federal-law trigger condition has been satisfied since the original research pass. DOJ and DHS published an interim final rule implementing the federal SAFER SKIES Act's Counter-UAS Authority for State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Law Enforcement and Correctional Agencies in the Federal Register on July 6, 2026 (effective July 1, 2026), establishing the detection/warning and mitigation certification framework this Indiana article's own trigger provision (Chapter 1) requires. Independent secondary reporting states Indiana's own state-law authority 'became effective' March 4, 2026 in anticipation of this federal action. However, direct confirmation that the Governor has published the required notice in the Indiana Register (the second half of the state-law trigger) was not located in this pass -- confirm current operational status directly with the Indiana State Police before assuming active counter-UAS detection or mitigation operations are underway at any specific Indiana site.

issuing_authority: Indiana Professional Licensing Agency / Indiana State Board of Registration for Professional Surveyors
source_title: 'Practice of Surveying' -- General Definition, Specific Non-Surveying Exemptions (Subsection (d)), and Photogrammetry/Remote-Sensing Supervision Requirement (Subsection (e))
citation: IC 25-21.5-1-7 (Indiana Land Surveyors licensing statute, Definitions)
effective_date: Unknown original enactment date; definitions section subsequently amended
binding_level: Binding (general licensing framework only -- no UAS-specific rule or guidance identified)
uas_topic: General professional-licensing competency for photogrammetric/GNSS survey methods (no UAS-specific rule or guidance located)
regulated_party: Licensed Professional Surveyors; persons performing survey-grade measurement of boundaries, fixed works, or topography
regulated_activity: Practicing land surveying -- including photogrammetric- or GNSS-based determination of boundaries, fixed works, or topography intended to be authoritative -- without licensure or outside an applicable statutory exemption
requirement_type: Licensure requirement for work performed 'under the responsible charge' of a professional surveyor, subject to a statutory exemption pathway (subsection (d)) for defined circumstances
permit_or_approval_required: License (PLS) generally required for boundary-related or authoritative topographic surveying work; a subsection (d) exemption may remove certain UAS-derived deliverables from the licensure requirement if its conditions are met
summary: IC 25-21.5-1-7 defines the 'practice of surveying' broadly to include making geometric measurements of, and gathering information about, the physical or legal features of the earth or the space above it, and developing that information into survey products. Subsection (c) lists activities -- including 'the creation of maps and geo-referenced data bases representing authoritative locations for boundaries, fixed works, or topography, either by terrestrial surveying methods or by photogrammetric or GNSS locations' -- that must be accomplished under the responsible charge of a professional surveyor unless specifically exempted under subsection (d). This retrofit pass fetched and read subsections (d) and (e) directly against Justia's codification for the first time (the original pass located only the general framework via a secondary aggregator, LawServer). Subsection (d) lists nine specific categories NOT included in the practice of surveying, most relevant to AEC UAS work: general maps prepared as guides or illustrative/educational tools (not clearly the same as authoritative boundary work); transcription of previously geo-referenced data into a GIS where the data are 'clearly not intended to indicate the authoritative location of property boundaries, the precise definition of the shape or contour of the earth, and the precise location of fixed works'; inventory maps/databases of an organization's own physical features/facilities/infrastructure, provided the data carry appropriate metadata (accuracy, compilation method, source, date) and disclaimers that they are not survey products; and maps/data depicting natural resources prepared by foresters, geologists, soil scientists, biologists, or similarly qualified non-surveyor professionals. Separately, and previously unlocated in the original pass, subsection (e) provides that 'the use of photogrammetric methods or similar remote sensing technology to perform any part of the practice of surveying... may be performed only under the direct control and supervision of a professional surveyor or professional photogrammetrist who maintain[s] a current title of "Certified Photogrammetrist" from a national scientific organization having a process for certifying photogrammetrists' -- a specific, previously unflagged supervision requirement directly applicable to UAS-derived photogrammetric survey products. No standalone Indiana Professional Licensing Agency or State Board of Registration for Professional Surveyors rule, advisory opinion, or FAQ specifically addressing UAS platforms (as distinct from photogrammetric methods generally) was located during this research pass.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Classify each UAS-derived deliverable against subsections (c) through (e) before mobilization, not just the general competency framework. If the product is intended to establish an authoritative boundary, fixed-works, or topographic location (orthomosaics, geo-referenced surface models, boundary-adjacent products), it must be produced under the responsible charge of a licensed PLS, OR under the direct control and supervision of a professional surveyor or a nationally certified photogrammetrist per subsection (e) -- a distinct, separately-applicable supervision requirement for photogrammetric/remote-sensing methods. If the product is a general-purpose, non-authoritative map or an internal facility-inventory database with appropriate metadata and disclaimers (subsection (d)), it may fall outside licensed practice, but document that classification decision and its basis in the project file.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Before relying on an unlicensed or exempt delivery path, give Indiana Professional Licensing Agency / Indiana State Board of Registration for Professional Surveyors a written description of the proposed UAS-derived product, its stated accuracy, and whether it will establish or certify boundaries, elevations, or authoritative locations -- and separately confirm whether subsection (e)'s photogrammetrist-supervision requirement is satisfied by the proposed production workflow, since it applies independently of the subsection (c)/(d) authoritative-location analysis. Retain the board's response with the project quality plan.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified

summary: Governor Mike Braun signed Executive Order 25-73 (on or about October 29-30, 2025), establishing the 'Indiana Initiative for Drone Dominance Task Force,' a multi-agency, university, and industry body directed to develop a strategic plan supporting federal 'American drone dominance' policy, drawing on assets such as NSWC Crane, Camp Atterbury, and Muscatatuck Urban Training Center. Stated priorities include a cross-sector aerial test corridor connecting these sites, expanding public-safety UAS applications at major events, strengthening Indiana's drone manufacturing supply chain (including smaller and emerging firms), and exploring counter-UAS detection/tracking/neutralization infrastructure. The task force owed its strategic plan and recommendations to the Governor by July 31, 2026. In a related development, Indiana was designated a national drone test site in January 2026 (Indiana Capital Chronicle, WFYI, WBIW), consistent with the task force's aerial-test-corridor priority. A search in this retrofit pass (conducted one week after the July 31, 2026 statutory deadline) did not locate a published version of the task force's completed strategic plan; its current status should be confirmed directly with the Governor's office or the Indiana Economic Development Corporation.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This order does not itself impose an operator-facing requirement, but AEC firms with drone-manufacturing, testing, or supply-chain interests should monitor the task force's strategic plan (due July 31, 2026, status not yet confirmed as published) for emerging state incentive programs, test-corridor access opportunities, or related state initiatives.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: No current state equipment restriction or incentive program is established by this order alone. Monitor the task force's strategic plan for any resulting state-level manufacturing, procurement, or supply-chain program relevant to fleet decisions.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat this as a policy-development and coordination vehicle, not a source of operator-facing legal obligations. Confirm the task force's current status and any resulting legislative or administrative action directly with the Governor's office before advising a client on state drone-industry incentives.
